title: Normal rings descend along faithfully flat ring maps
statement: Let $R\to S$ be a faithfully flat homomorphism of commutative rings [def-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ring-map]. If $S$ is a normal ring [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], then $R$ is a normal ring: if every prime localization $S_{\mathfrak q}$ is a domain integrally closed in its fraction field, then so is every prime localization $R_{\mathfrak p}$. No Noetherian, domain, finite-type or locality hypothesis is imposed; the zero ring is not faithfully flat over a nonzero ring, and $R=S=0$ is permitted (no primes).

proof.text: Let $f:R\to S$ be the given faithfully flat map. It is flat by [def-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ring-map]. Fix a prime $\mathfrak p\subset R$. By [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-surjective-spectrum] choose a prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$ such that $f^{-1}(\mathfrak q)=\mathfrak p$.

Put $A=R_{\mathfrak p}$ and $B=S_{\mathfrak q}$. By [lem-weil-pbc-flat-local-ring-maps], the map $g:A\to B$, $r/t\mapsto f(r)/f(t)$, is a flat local homomorphism of local rings. Only the flatness clause is used, not the optional Noetherian clause. By [lem-weil-pbc-flat-local-hom-faithfully-flat], $g$ is faithfully flat. Since $S$ is normal, [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring] says that $B$ is a domain integrally closed in its fraction field.

proof.text: By the injectivity clause of [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ideal-contraction] applied to $g$, the map $g$ is injective. Hence $A$ is a domain: $1_A=0_A$ would imply $1_B=0_B$, contrary to $B$ being a domain; and if $uv=0$ then $g(u)g(v)=0$, so the domain property of $B$ and injectivity give $u=0$ or $v=0$.

source.place: Tag 033G (lemma-descent-normal), sentence proving the local source is a domain; Tag 05CK (lemma-faithfully-flat-universally-injective).

proof.text: Let $x=a/b\in\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ with $b\ne0$ be integral over $A$, so $x^n+c_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+c_0=0$ for some $c_i\in A$. The formula $u/v\mapsto g(u)/g(v)$ defines an injective ring map $\operatorname{Frac}(A)\to\operatorname{Frac}(B)$: denominators remain nonzero by injectivity of $g$, equality of fractions is cross multiplication, and a fraction maps to zero only if its numerator is zero. Applying this map to the displayed equation shows that $y=g(a)/g(b)$ satisfies the monic equation with coefficients $g(c_i)\in B$. Integral closedness of $B$, in the explicit sense of [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring], therefore gives $s\in B$ with $y=s/1$. Cross multiplication gives $g(a)=g(b)s$.

source.place: Tag 033G (lemma-descent-normal), sentences beginning Next, suppose that a/b is integral and Then a/b in S; Tag 0309 (definition-domain-normal).

proof.text: The ideal $(bA)B$ generated by the images of $bA$ is exactly $g(b)B$: each generator $g(br)=g(b)g(r)$ is a multiple of $g(b)$, and $g(b)$ itself is one of the generators. Thus $g(a)=g(b)s$ implies $g(a)\in(bA)B$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-ideal-contraction] to $g$ and the ideal $bA$ to obtain $a\in bA$. Choose $r\in A$ with $a=br$. Since $b\ne0$, $x=a/b=r/1$ in $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$.

Every element of $\operatorname{Frac}(A)$ integral over $A$ thus belongs to $A$. Together with Step 3 this says that $R_{\mathfrak p}=A$ is a normal domain. Since $\mathfrak p$ was arbitrary, [def-weil-pbc-normal-ring] says that $R$ is normal. If $R=0$ there are no prime ideals, and the assertion is vacuous; unitality forces $S=0$ as well. Conversely a faithfully flat map $R\to0$ forces $R=0$ by the injectivity clause already cited. No assertion that the unlocalized ring $R$ is a domain was used.

Step 4: the map Frac(A)→Frac(B) is well defined, the transported equation stays monic, and g(a)=g(b)s; this is a few lines from the definitions, so the elementary flag is justified. Step 5: (bA)B=g(b)B, and the 05CK leaf gives a∈bA. Step 6: both zero-ring cases are vacuous. All four tools are existing Mathlib leaves (sk-thm-p1), so no tool_uses entry is needed.
